hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a Kenyan secondary school compound: a long row of blue-roofed classrooms with open doors, a green playing field with two goalposts, a round water tank, shady trees, a school gate and a sunny sky.
hero.alt: A drawing of a school compound with a row of classrooms, a playing field, a water tank, trees and a gate.

slides.title: Think bigger: what is above a single cell?
slides.subtitle: Write or draw your own idea. Work alone and in silence.
slides.time_note: 4 minutes silent writing, 1 minute to set up

blocks.text: Are these four cells acting alone, or part of something bigger?

items: droplet :: Platelet
magnifier :: Neutrophil
link :: Fibroblast
bandage :: Epidermal cell

do: Display the four wound-healing cell drawings from learners' Version 3 models, next to the prompt.
Learners work alone in their ARES notebooks. No talking.
Start the 4 minute timer.
Walk round and scan 6 to 8 notebooks. Do not comment on what you see.
Note any learner whose prediction has no structure above the cell. Pair that learner with a stronger peer for the Observe phase.
say: Look carefully at these four cells. We have studied each one. Today I want you to think BIGGER.
Before I teach you anything new, draw or write what you predict exists ABOVE the level of a single cell. Say why you think so.
You have 4 minutes of silent thinking time. Go.
look_for: Scan 6 to 8 notebooks. Each has a written or sketched prediction that names at least one level above the cell, such as 'group of cells', 'layer of skin' or 'body system'.
Note who drew a cluster of cells, who drew the whole body, and who left the page blank. You will use this for cold-calling.
if_then: If a learner has written nothing after 2 minutes, say quietly: 'Draw one of the cells. Now draw what it might be sitting inside.'
If a learner writes only 'cells', say: 'What are the cells part of? Add one idea.'
Do not say if an idea is right or wrong. Predictions are corrected later by evidence.
notes.why_this_works: Writing a prediction alone, before any teaching, makes each learner commit to an idea. They then care about the evidence. The common idea that each cell works alone is brought into the open here and tested later.
answer_key: Model answer: I think the four cells are part of something bigger. Many cells of the same kind group together to make a layer of skin. The skin is part of the body.

slides.title: Share with your partner
slides.subtitle: Elbow partner. 90 seconds. Both of you speak.
slides.time_note: 90 seconds pair talk, 30 seconds to move

items: people :: Turn to your elbow partner
speech :: Share your prediction and say why
ear :: Listen to your partner's idea

do: Start the 90 second timer.
Walk round and listen. Choose three pairs to share on the next slide: one pair who drew a tissue-like cluster, one who drew the whole body, and one who was unsure.
Do not correct any idea.
say: Turn to your elbow partner. Share your prediction and say why you think so.
You have 90 seconds. Both partners speak.
look_for: Every pair has both partners talking.
Listen for words such as 'group', 'layer', 'body' or 'system'. Listen to at least 5 pairs.
if_then: If a pair is silent, say: 'Tell your partner one thing you drew or wrote. Then ask your partner one question.'
If a pair finishes early, say: 'Now find one way your ideas are different.'
notes.why_this_works: Talking in pairs lets every learner rehearse an idea in a safe space. Learners are then more willing to speak in front of the class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: We record ideas. We do not say right or wrong yet.
slides.time_note: 3 minutes: three pairs share, teacher records

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Hold these ideas. We test them today.

do: Cold-call 3 pairs: first the pair who drew a tissue-like cluster, then the pair who drew the whole body, then the pair who were unsure. You want a range of ideas.
Ask each pair: 'What was your reasoning?'
Write the key prediction words on the board in a column headed 'PREDICT'. Do not confirm or deny. Likely words: tissue, group, system, organ, body.
Take a quick hands-up count: 'Who thinks the four cells work alone?' 'Who thinks they are part of something bigger?' Write both numbers on the board to return to in Explain.
say: Look at the finger that healed. Four kinds of cell helped. Are they alone, or part of something bigger?
Pair one, what was your reasoning?
Hold these predictions. We are going to test them against evidence right now.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after each question before you choose a pair
look_for: Each of the 3 pairs gives a reason, not only an answer.
The PREDICT column has at least 3 different words from learners.
Note the hands-up counts for 'alone' and 'something bigger'.
if_then: If a pair gives only an answer, say: 'Tell us one thing you saw in the cells that made you think so.'
If a learner asks 'Am I right?', say: 'We will find out from the evidence. Hold your idea.'
Do not correct any prediction. A learner who hears 'wrong' now may stop thinking.
notes.why_this_works: A public record of predictions lets the class see its own thinking change later. Not correcting keeps learners willing to share honest ideas.

slides.title: Evidence Card Set 10
slides.subtitle: Two sides. Use evidence from the cards, not guesses.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes to hand out and explain

blocks.text: A drawing of a school compound with a row of classrooms, a playing field, a water tank, trees and a gate.
items: school_compound_organisation

A friendly flat cartoon of a Kenyan secondary school compound: a long row of blue-roofed classrooms with open doors, a green playing field with two goalposts, a round water tank, shady trees, a school gate and a sunny sky.
Side A :: Pictures from biology
Side B :: Pictures from a school

do: Put learners in groups of 4. Give each group one Evidence Card Set 10 (printed or on screen).
Do not show the hierarchy diagram slide in Explain until groups have finished their tables.
Keep this slide short. The work is on the next slide.
say: On Side A you have real microscope images from biology.
On Side B you have a school picture I want you to think about.
Your job in your group is to fill in the Observation Table. Use evidence from the cards, not guesses.
look_for: Every group has a card set and a pencil ready.
Pair any learner whose prediction had no structure above the cell with a stronger peer.
if_then: If you do not have enough printed sets, say: 'Two groups will share one set. Pass it over after 7 minutes.'
If you have no printed set at all, show Side A and Side B on the projector and read each card aloud. Learners copy what they need.
notes.why_this_works: Learners meet familiar school life and the new biology side by side. The school side gives them a picture of how many similar units make one working whole.

slides.title: Your turn: complete the Observation Table
slides.subtitle: Groups of 4. Use evidence from the cards. Write in your own book.

do: Start the 15 minute timer.

Learners copy the table into their own books if needed. The first column is the level of organisation, the second is the biological example from wound healing, the third is the school analogy, the fourth is the function at this level.
Circulate. At 5 minutes check whether groups link epidermal cell, epithelial tissue, skin and integumentary system.
If a group is stuck, ask the question below. Do NOT give the answer.
At 10 minutes tell two groups to be ready to share their Function column.
At 15 minutes collect one table per group for quick review before Explain.
say: Your job is to fill in the Observation Table. Biological example, school analogy, and the function at each level.
Look at image 2 on Side A. What has changed compared to image 1? What is made up of many of the same cell?
Two groups, please be ready to share your Function column. What does the tissue do that the single cell cannot do alone?
notes.wait_time: 30 seconds at 10 minutes for the two groups to confirm their answer
look_for: The table has all biological levels with a matching school example and a stated function for each. Mastery: at least 3 of 4 biological levels correct with a function.
Check every group's table as you collect them. Check that learners fill in the function column, not only the names.
if_then: If a group is stuck, say: 'Look at image 2 on Side A. What has changed compared to image 1? What is made up of many of the same cell?'
If a group writes only names and no function, say: 'What job does this level do that the level below cannot do alone?'
If a group guesses without the cards, say: 'Show me the card that tells you that.'
notes.why_this_works: The school column gives learners a familiar pattern: many similar units form one working whole. They find the pattern before they are given the biology words.
answer_key: Row 1: Cell | single epidermal cell | one student at Mwangaza Secondary School | does one small job, for example forms part of the skin surface.
Row 2: Tissue | many epidermal cells together (epithelial tissue) | a class of 42 students | the same cells work together as one layer to cover and protect the surface.
Row 3: Organ | the skin (epidermis, dermis and hypodermis) | Mwangaza Secondary School | different tissues work together to protect the body.
Row 4: Organ system | the integumentary system (skin, hair, nails, sweat glands) | Nairobi County Education System | a group of organs works together to protect the body.
Row 5: Organism | the whole human body | Kenyan society | all systems work together so the person lives, grows and heals.

slides.title: Share: what does a tissue do?
slides.subtitle: Listen to other groups. Do you agree?

blocks.text: What does the TISSUE do that a single cell cannot do alone?

items: raised_hand :: Two groups read their rows aloud
ear :: Listen. Do you agree?
pencil :: Fix your own table if needed

do: Cold-call 2 groups to read their completed rows aloud. Choose one group that finished early and one group that was stuck at the 5 minute check.
Correct any factual errors immediately using the board.
Learners fix their own tables.
Keep the collected tables for review before Explain.
say: Group one, read your rows aloud.
Group two, do you agree? What would you add?
What does the tissue do that a single cell cannot do alone?
look_for: The two groups state a function for each level, not only a name.
At least 3 of the 4 biological levels are correct in the tables you review.
if_then: If a group mixes up organ and organ system, say: 'An organ is one structure like the skin. An organ system is a group of organs working together. Which one is the integumentary system?'
If a group says the school IS an organ, say: 'The school is like an organ. It is not an organ. What is the same?'
notes.why_this_works: Hearing other groups lets learners test their own thinking against evidence. Fixing errors on the board stops wrong ideas before the explanation.
answer_key: A tissue is many cells of the same type working together as one layer. Together they can cover and protect a surface, which one cell cannot do alone.

slides.title: Check your predictions
slides.subtitle: Look at the PREDICT column. Mark your own idea.

items: raised_hand :: Who predicted tissue, or a group of the same cells?
raised_hand :: Who predicted organ or system?
pencil :: Mark your prediction right or wrong in a different colour

do: Point to the PREDICT column on the board.
Ask the two hands-up questions. Count and compare with the counts from Predict.
Learners mark their own prediction in their notebook in a different colour. Part right counts as part right.
say: Let's check your predictions. Who predicted the word tissue, or a group of the same cells? Raise your hand.
Who predicted organ or system?
Your predictions were strong. Here is what the evidence confirms.
look_for: Every learner has marked their prediction in a different colour. Check 6 notebooks.
Learners who thought cells work alone now say they changed their mind.
if_then: If a learner marks everything wrong because the words differ, say: 'Part right counts. Which part matches the evidence?'
If a learner is upset about being wrong, say: 'A prediction is a first idea. Scientists change ideas when the evidence changes.'
notes.why_this_works: Marking their own prediction shows learners how their thinking has changed. This helps with the idea that each cell works alone.
answer_key: Model answer: My prediction said 'a group of cells'. The evidence shows that is right. I add 'organ' and 'system' in green.

slides.title: What do the pictures share?
slides.subtitle: Think first. Names come after the ideas.

blocks.text: What do the school picture and the microscope image have in common?

items: Image 2 compared with image 1: what changed?
What do many of the same cell do together?
How do different groups join to make skin?

do: Ask the questions one at a time. Click one at a time.
Cold-call 1 learner for the first question: choose someone who predicted 'group' or 'tissue'.
Take answers from the table notes. Do not name the levels yet. Wait for learners to describe each idea.
say: Epithelial tissue: what do the school analogy and the microscope image have in common?
Image 2 compared with image 1. What changed?
What do many of the same cell do together?
look_for: Learners describe 'many of the same units working together' in their own words.
Listen to at least 4 different learners.
if_then: If no one answers, say: 'Look at your class. Forty-two students. What are they together?'
If someone gives only a name, say: 'Tell me what it does, not only what it is called.'
notes.why_this_works: Small questions let learners build the idea step by step. They understand what a level does before they are given its name.
answer_key: Both show many similar units working together as one group. One student is like one cell. A class is like a tissue.

slides.title: The hierarchy: cell to organism
slides.subtitle: Five levels. Each level adds something new.
slides.time_note: 3 minutes, one level at a time

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Draw or reveal the hierarchy one level at a time. Pause after each level.
At the Cell level write platelet, neutrophil, fibroblast and epidermal cell.
Then add the wound-healing examples as learners contribute: epithelial tissue, skin, integumentary system, human body.
Link each level to its school match: class, school, county education system, Kenyan society.
Optional: preview the ARES video 'Cells and organisms' first. It may not match this lesson exactly.
say: Epithelial tissue is a group of the same cells working together. What do the school analogy and the microscope image have in common?
Many tissues together make an organ, like the skin.
Organs working together make an organ system. The skin, hair, nails and sweat glands are the integumentary system.
All the systems together make the whole organism. Here, it is the student in Nairobi who cut a finger.
look_for: Learners say organ and organ system correctly. Listen to at least 4 learners.
Learners link each level to the healing cut, not only the names.
if_then: If a learner mixes organ and organ system, say: 'An organ is one structure like the skin. An organ system is a group of organs working together. Which one is the integumentary system?'
If a learner says the school IS an organ, say: 'The school is like an organ. Is it the same thing? What is different?'
notes.why_this_works: Naming each level after learners meet the idea helps the words stay. The shared diagram on the board gives every learner the same picture before they write.
notes.science_note: The school picture matches the order of the levels, not every detail. A school is like an organ, but it is not an organ. A student can leave a class. A cell cannot choose to leave its tissue.

slides.title: Explain it in your own words
slides.subtitle: Use the healing cut. Write 5 sentences. Silent and alone.
slides.time_note: 8 minutes silent writing, 1 minute to set up

blocks.text: Why can one epidermal cell not heal a wound on its own? What levels must work together to restore the finger?

items: Claim :: Answer the question
Evidence :: The levels of organisation from the cards
Reasoning :: What each level adds

do: Start the 8 minute timer.
Learners write in their notebooks, alone and in silence.
Circulate and read over shoulders. Read 4 to 6 notebooks.
After 4 minutes, prompt any learner with fewer than 3 sentences.
Give a prompt card to any learner who mixes up organ and organ system.
say: Now I want this in YOUR words, in YOUR notebook. Write 5 sentences. Use the healing cut.
Explain why one cell is not enough, and what each level adds. Eight minutes, silent, individual writing. Go.
look_for: Read 4 to 6 notebooks. Each names at least 3 levels of organisation, mentions the healing cut, and states a function for at least one level.
Check that each answer has a claim, evidence and reasoning.
if_then: If a learner has fewer than 3 sentences after 4 minutes, say quietly: 'What does the tissue do that one cell cannot? Write that.'

If a learner mixes organ and organ system, give the prompt card: 'An ORGAN is one structure like the skin. An ORGAN SYSTEM is a group of organs working together, like the integumentary system. Can you revise sentence 3?'
If a learner writes only 'cells work together', say: 'Which levels? Name them, in order.'
notes.why_this_works: Writing a claim, evidence and reasoning makes learners join the levels to the healing cut. It also shows which learners still think a single cell does the job.
answer_key: A single epidermal cell cannot heal a wound alone. Epidermal cells group together to form epithelial tissue, which can cover and seal the surface in a way one cell cannot. The tissue is part of the skin, an organ made of different tissues that protects the finger. The skin belongs to the integumentary system, a group of organs working together to protect the whole body. Healing needs platelets, neutrophils, fibroblasts and epidermal cells working together inside all these levels, so the finger is restored.

slides.title: Does our explanation match the evidence?
slides.subtitle: Show with your thumb.

blocks.text: Does this explanation match our evidence?

items: check :: Thumbs up: it matches
question :: Thumbs sideways: partly
cross :: Thumbs down: it does not match

do: Cold-call 2 learners with strong responses to read aloud. Choose one who named all five levels and one who linked a level to the healing cut.
Ask the class to show a thumb.
Address any thumbs down. Ask that learner what is missing.
say: Read your explanation aloud, please.
Does this explanation match our evidence? Thumbs up, thumbs down or thumbs sideways.
Thumbs down: tell us what is missing.
look_for: Most thumbs are up or sideways, with reasons.
Learners who still say a single cell can heal alone are few. Count thumbs and note them.
if_then: If many thumbs are sideways, say: 'Which level is not clear? Show me with the diagram.'
If a learner says thumbs down but cannot say why, say: 'Look at the five levels. Which one is missing?'
notes.why_this_works: Checking an explanation against evidence makes learners judge the idea, not the speaker. This helps correct the idea that a single cell heals a wound alone.
answer_key: Model answer: Thumbs up. It names the levels in the right order. It uses the healing cut and says what the tissue does that one cell cannot.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: what do we know now?
slides.subtitle: Two notes. Three minutes. Write quietly.

items: YELLOW note :: NOW WE KNOW. One thing today's evidence answers.
BLUE note :: NEW QUESTIONS. One new question from today.

do: Give each learner two sticky notes: yellow and blue (or ARES digital cards).
Learners write alone for 3 minutes.
Learners post both notes on the Driving Question Board, yellow under 'NOW WE KNOW' and blue under 'NEW QUESTIONS'.
While they write, scan for vague yellow notes.
say: The Driving Question asks why cells look different and how shape determines job. Today we zoomed out.
On your YELLOW note, write one thing we can now answer because of what we saw today.
On your BLUE note, write one new question this lesson has opened up for you. You have 3 minutes.
look_for: Check at least 8 yellow notes. Each names a level of organisation and uses something seen on the cards today, not 'I learned about cells'.
Blue notes are questions that look forward, not just repeat today's content.
if_then: If a yellow note is vague, say: 'Which level of organisation did you learn about? Add one example from the cards.' Give that learner a 1 minute check-in.
If a blue note is only a restatement, say: 'What do you not know yet about how these levels work together?'
notes.why_this_works: Posting what we know and what we wonder makes learning visible. Evidence notes tied to today's cards stop learners from copying textbook facts.
answer_key: Yellow: Now I know tissues form because similar epidermal cells group together to do one job, as in a class of 42 students.
Blue: How do the skin and the immune system send signals to each other?

slides.title: Does today's evidence support our claim?
slides.subtitle: Look at the board. Then vote.
slides.time_note: 3 minutes: reading notes and class vote

blocks.text: Claim: no single cell heals a cut finger alone. Does today's evidence support it?

items: check :: Yes, the evidence supports it
question :: Not sure yet
cross :: No, the evidence does not support it

do: Read 5 or 6 notes aloud. Group similar ones by theme: structural organisation, function, and how organ systems communicate.
Point to the board and show how far the class has come since Lesson 1.
Run a quick hands-up vote on the claim. Write the numbers on the board.
say: I notice several of you are now asking how organ systems communicate with each other. Does the integumentary system send signals to the immune system? That is a brilliant question. We will return to it in Strand 3 when we study animal physiology.
This board is growing. We started with one cut finger. Now we understand the organisation behind it.
Hands up if the evidence supports the claim. Hands up if you are not sure.
look_for: Most hands support the claim. Ask two learners to name one piece of evidence from today.
Learners cite something seen on the cards, not a textbook fact. Listen to at least 3 learners.
if_then: If a learner votes 'no' or 'not sure', say: 'Which level could do the job alone? Show me on the diagram.'
If a learner gives textbook evidence, say: 'What did you see on the cards today that shows this?'
notes.why_this_works: A vote makes learners decide whether evidence supports a claim. Clustering notes helps learners see patterns in what the class wonders.
answer_key: Model answer: Yes. The cards show the epidermal cell, the tissue, the skin and the body system. Each level does a job the level below cannot do alone.

slides.title: Model Version 4: a hierarchy diagram
slides.subtitle: Version 4 organises your earlier work. It does not replace it.

blocks.text: This is a drawing of the five tiers. Your own model fills each tier.

do: Learners take out their cumulative cell model, Versions 1 to 3.
Display a blank template on the board with five labelled tiers and blank boxes at each level.
Tell learners to use a NEW colour for Version 4.
say: Take out your cumulative model, Versions 1 through 3. Look at the cells you drew.
Today we zoom ALL the way out. Version 4 is a hierarchy diagram. It does not replace your earlier work. It organises it.
I want to see your cells from Version 3 sitting inside their tissue, inside their organ, inside their system, inside the whole organism.
look_for: Every learner has their Versions 1 to 3 out and a new colour ready.
if_then: If a learner has lost their earlier model, say: 'Redraw two cells quickly from memory. Use them for Version 4.'
notes.why_this_works: Keeping one model for the whole unit shows learners how their thinking grows. A new colour each lesson makes each revision easy to see.

slides.title: Build Version 4: nest your cells in the hierarchy
slides.subtitle: Alone. 12 minutes. Use a new colour.

items: Cell: 2 or more healing cells
Tissue they belong to
Organ the tissues form
Organ system, then organism
Each level's job in healing

blocks.text: Model Revision Note: What does Version 4 show that Version 3 did not?
items: This model is based on evidence from…

do: Start the 12 minute timer.
Learners write the sentence starter 'This model is based on evidence from…' in their Model Revision Note.
Circulate and give targeted feedback.
At 6 minutes, check that two cell types and a tissue label are present. Tell learners to do those first if they are missing.
Give a structured scaffold card for homework to any learner who only completes 3 levels.
say: You have 12 minutes. Every level must be labelled AND must include the function in wound healing, not just the name.
At the bottom, write your Model Revision Note: what does Version 4 show that Version 3 could not show?
Check: can I see two cell types at the Cell level? Can I see a tissue label? If not, do those now.
notes.wait_time: The full 12 minutes, with a check at 6 minutes
look_for: Check at least 8 models. Version 4 has all five levels in the right order, at least 2 named wound-healing cells at the Cell level, and a function at each level. Mastery: 4 of 5 levels correct with function.
The Model Revision Note mentions the hierarchy and cites evidence. Check that learners nest their Version 3 cells and do not start from scratch.
if_then: If a learner redraws all cells, say: 'Use the cells you already drew. Put them inside the tissue box.'
If a learner lists names only, say: 'What does this level DO in wound healing? Write that beside the name.'
If a learner only completes 3 levels, give the homework scaffold card: 'Complete the missing two levels: what tissue do neutrophils belong to? What organ system do they help protect?'
notes.why_this_works: Putting earlier cells inside the new hierarchy makes learning build on itself. The revision note makes learners say what the new model explains that the old one could not.
answer_key: Cell: epidermal cell (divides and moves to close the surface) and neutrophil (engulfs bacteria).
Tissue: epidermal cells form epithelial tissue, which covers and protects the surface. Neutrophils are blood cells, so they belong to blood tissue.
Organ: the skin, made of different tissues, protects the finger.
Organ system: the integumentary system (skin, hair, nails, sweat glands) works together to protect the body.
Organism: the whole human body, the student in Nairobi, healed by all levels working together.

Model Revision Note: Version 4 shows how my cells fit inside tissues, organs and systems. Version 3 showed single cells only. This model is based on evidence from the Evidence Card Set 10 and the hierarchy diagram.

slides.title: Share, revise and look ahead
slides.subtitle: Hold up your model. Add one idea. Predict what comes next.
slides.time_note: 1 minute sharing, 2 minutes silent revision, 1 minute to write

items: megaphone :: Two learners hold up and tell about their model
pencil :: What could you add? Revise in your new colour
thought :: Write one sentence: what will we do next?

blocks.text: Next lesson I think we will… because…

do: Cold-call 2 learners to hold up and narrate their Version 4 model. Choose one with a complete model and one who found it hard.
Ask the class what they included that others might want to add.
Give 2 minutes of silent revision in the new colour.
Learners write a one-sentence prediction for the next lesson.
Collect models, or photograph them for the ARES digital portfolio.
say: Hold up your model and tell us what it shows.
What did they include that you might want to add or revise?
Revise your model now in your new colour. Then write one sentence: what do you predict we will do next lesson?
look_for: Check at least 6 models after revision. Learners added or fixed at least one level.
Each learner has written a one-sentence prediction for the next lesson.
if_then: If a learner cannot write a prediction, say: 'Look at your model. What is still missing from the story of how cells work together?'
If a learner is stuck on revision, say: 'Look at your partner's model. Find one thing they did that you did not.'
notes.why_this_works: Hearing other models helps learners spot gaps in their own. A prediction for the next lesson links today's learning to what comes next.
answer_key: Model answer: Next lesson I think we will put all our models together, because we now know how cells, tissues, organs and systems fit together.

build_log.sow_says: A Form 1 student in Nairobi cuts their finger (unit phenomenon); 'one Form 2 student at Mwangaza Secondary School, Nairobi'; 'Form 2 Class of 42 students'
build_log.deck_does: Slides say 'student' and 'class of 42 students'. The Form 1 / Form 2 wording stays only in the SoW, not on slides. Notes say 'the student in Nairobi'.
build_log.why: CBE uses Grade, not Form. The SoW terms should be updated by the SoW owner.

build_log.sow_says: Lesson header 'Sub-Strand 1.1: Cell Structure'; unit data says 'Sub-Strand 1.3: Cell Structure and Specialisation'
build_log.deck_does: Uses no sub-strand number on Part A slides.
build_log.why: The sub-strand number does not match between the lesson and the unit data.

build_log.slide: Think bigger: what is above a single cell?
build_log.sow_says: four labelled cells from the wound-healing phenomenon (platelet, neutrophil, fibroblast, epidermal cell — drawings from their own Version 3 models)
build_log.deck_does: Shows the four cell names as tiles and asks learners to use their Version 3 drawings.
build_log.why: Lessons 3 to 9 do not clearly have learners draw platelets, neutrophils or fibroblasts in Versions 1 to 3 (Lesson 8 lists red and white blood cells, nerve, sperm and muscle cells). Learners may have no such drawings. The SoW owner should check.

build_log.slide: Your turn: complete the Observation Table
build_log.sow_says: Side A has four images ending at the integumentary system in a body outline; the Observation Table has 'Level of Organisation | Biological Example | School Analogy | Function' while Side B has five school levels, and the mastery threshold is '3 of 4 levels'
build_log.deck_does: Table has five rows (cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism). Answer key row 5 uses the whole human body, which is shown only as the body outline in image 4. Mastery check stays '3 of 4 biological levels'.
build_log.why: Five school levels and four biological images do not match. The SoW owner should say how many rows the table has.

build_log.slide: Your turn: complete the Observation Table
build_log.sow_says: skin as an organ (epidermis + dermis + hypodermis layers labelled)
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the three layers in the answer key as the SoW says.
build_log.why: Many textbooks describe the skin as epidermis and dermis, with the hypodermis as the tissue below the skin. A teacher should check.

build_log.sow_says: showing the four wound-healing cell types (platelet, neutrophil, fibroblast, epidermal cell) nested inside epithelial tissue → skin → integumentary system → human body
build_log.deck_does: Shows the five levels and lists all four cells at the Cell level, as the SoW says.
build_log.why: Only epidermal cells form epithelial tissue. Platelets (cell fragments, not whole cells) and neutrophils are in blood, and fibroblasts are in connective tissue. A teacher should check.

build_log.slide: Build Version 4: nest your cells in the hierarchy

lesson_oneliner: No single cell heals a cut finger alone. Cells work together in bigger and bigger groups.
purpose: Learners trace how cells are organised into tissues, organs, organ systems and the whole organism. They use the healing cut as the example.
Learners find the pattern first from the evidence cards and the school picture. The level names come after they understand the idea.
This matters because tissues and organs are the main units of study in later strands on plants and animals.
The lesson links the four wound-healing cells (platelet, neutrophil, fibroblast, epidermal cell) to the levels above the cell.
Common misconception: each cell works alone, or a school IS an organ. The prediction, the evidence cards, the thumbs check and the science note on the hierarchy slide address this.
before_class: Print or load Evidence Card Set 10 (Side A biology images, Side B school analogy). One set per group of 4.
Check learners have their cumulative cell model, Versions 1 to 3, and a new colour for Version 4.
Prepare two sticky notes per learner, one yellow and one blue, or ARES digital cards.
Prepare the Driving Question Board with columns 'NOW WE KNOW' and 'NEW QUESTIONS'.
Draw a 'PREDICT' column on the board. Keep space for the hierarchy diagram and a blank five-tier template.
Prepare a prompt card for organ versus organ system, and a homework scaffold card for Version 4.
If learners will cut any cards, have scissors ready and read the reminder in the build log.
Preview the optional ARES video 'Cells and organisms' before using it.
do_not_show: Do not show the slide 'The hierarchy: cell to organism' until groups have filled in and shared their Observation Table.
Do not show the slides 'Model Version 4: a hierarchy diagram' and 'Build Version 4' until the Driving Question Board slides are finished.
Do not play any ARES video on levels of organisation before learners have written their predictions.
so_far: We have studied cell parts, plant and animal cells, and specialised cells.
goals: Describe how cells are organised into tissues, organs, organ systems and an organism.
Build a hierarchy diagram using wound-healing examples.
Compare the levels with a Kenyan school.

resource_notes.note: Explains the body's levels of organisation, so it gives away the Predict answer. Show it after 'The hierarchy: cell to organism' as consolidation.
Cells-and-organisms exercise suits this topic but is a quiz. Preview it, and use it as a check after 'Explain it in your own words', not in Predict.
Respiratory system organs is not the skin or wound-healing example students analyse. It is too detailed for this lesson, so it does not fit the evidence set.
Cells and organisms fits the hierarchy discussion. Preview that it covers tissue, organ and organ system, and use it at 'The hierarchy: cell to organism'.
Digestive organs give a second example of organs forming a system. Use it after 'Explain it in your own words', or in Strand 3 on animal physiology.
Differentiation into somatic and germ cells answers a likely new question. Use it in Lesson 11 or 12, not at this DQB slide.
A general middle school biology introduction is too broad and below Grade 10. It does not help students build Version 4.

summary.observe_prompt: Describe the biology images and the school pictures you studied.
summary.learn_prompt: Say how cells are organised, from one cell to the whole body.
summary.explain_prompt: Say why no single cell can heal the cut finger alone.
summary.next_lesson: We put the whole cell story together in a poster model.
summary.answer_observe: Annotated microscope images and diagrams showed one epidermal cell, then epithelial tissue of many epidermal cells, then the skin as an organ cross-section, then the integumentary system in the human body. A matching school diagram showed one student, a class, Mwangaza Secondary School, Nairobi County Education and Kenyan society.
summary.answer_learn: Cells of the same type group together to form tissues. Different tissues combine to form organs. Organs working together form organ systems. Organ systems together make the whole organism. In wound healing, epidermal cells form epithelial tissue, part of the skin organ, which belongs to the integumentary system, which protects the whole organism.
summary.answer_explain: No single specialised cell, not the platelet, neutrophil, fibroblast or epidermal cell, can heal the cut finger alone. Healing needs all four cell types organised into tissues, organs and systems that coordinate their jobs. Shape decides job at the cell level, but organisation decides survival at the organism level.
reflection: Could learners tell an organ from an organ system without prompting? Did they confuse tissue and organ in their writing or models? If yes, plan a 5-minute retrieval sort at the start of Lesson 11.
Did the school analogy help, or did learners think a school IS an organ? Note which groups used it well and which dropped it.
Did learners nest their Version 3 cells inside the hierarchy, or redraw from scratch? If more than 30% started again, give a template next time.
Were the blue notes forward-looking questions, or restatements of today? What does this say about readiness for Strands 2 and 3?
Did learners link their explanations to the healing cut? If not, open Lesson 11 with the phenomenon image and ask where today's knowledge sits.
